newsitem.title: DENMARK: FOCUS - BA/AA plan has wide legal impact.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - BA/AA plan has wide legal impact.

text.p: Plans for a transatlantic alliance between British Airways and AMR Corp's American Airlines will have wide legal impacts on all inter-continental alliances to be vetted by the European Commission, legal experts said on Friday.

"The enormity in commercial and air-political terms of the BA/American Airlines alliance triggered a change in Brussels which could well have far-reaching consequences for all inter-continental alliances," said Phillipe Chappatte, a partner with lawyers Slaughter and May.
"The Commission will be keen to establish clear precedents for its powers of control over transatlantic alliances," Chappatte told a conference of the European Air Law Association.

The Commission announced its probe into the planned BA/American tie up in the summer, saying that its preliminary view of such deals was that they would "substantially restrict competition on the routes between the United States and Europe as well as on some intra-Community (EU) routes".

The two airlines agreed plans to coordinate operations on all of BA's 244 flights per week from Britain to its 22 U.S. destinations and all of American's 238 flights a week from seven home airports to 12 European destinations.

The Commission also opened parallel probes into deals between Germany's Lufthansa and United Airlines, between Scandinavia's SAS and United Airlines, Swissair/Beligum's Sabena /Austrian Airlines and Delta Air Lines Inc, Dutch airline KLM and Northwest Airlines Corp and between British Airways and USAir.

Commission investigations, the outcome of which Chappatte said was too far off to predict, means there are now three competition authorities looking into the BA/AA alliance, the others being the more traditional inquiries by British and U.S. anti-trust authorities.
"Hopefully, the three regulators will work out a sensible procedure and methodology so that the airlines concerned do not have to deal with conflicting regulatory approaches," Chappatte said.

Professor Prodromos Dagtoglou, EU Air Law Association president, said airlines had to make alliances, and go through the subsequent anti-trust inquiries, because of restrictions limiting foreign ownership of an airline to 25 percent in the United States and 49 percent in the European Union.
"Alliances remain the only alternative means to globalisation, which the airlines consider as essential in the long run," he said.
"Whether this globalisation will lead to lower fares, as the airlines claim, remains to be seen. The Commission authorities should take them at their word and insist on lower fares."
